stories.topic: Germany's Reparations, Hyperinflation and the Birth of GDP
stories.summary: After the First World War, the winning nations demanded reparations so high that Germany had no option but to print huge amounts of money. Prices ran so far out of control that what could buy a house one week would buy only a loaf of bread the next. The chaos fed the right-wing extremism that produced Adolf Hitler. Keynes, in The Economic Consequences of the Peace, argued that part of the problem was that nobody knew how wealthy a nation actually was, so the victors could make absurd demands. That gap created the demand for something like GDP, which did not yet exist.
stories.insight: Hyperinflation is a political catastrophe as much as an economic one. The story also shows that measurement is policy infrastructure: GDP was born because the world had made a disastrous demand of an economy it could not see.
stories.quote: one reason this happens is that we don't know national wealth. We don't know what's going on, and therefore we can make demands that are too crazy, as those demands were.

stories.topic: Checking Whether India's CPI Can Be Trusted
stories.summary: Ajay argues that weak state capability affects everything, statistics included, so all government data deserves great skepticism, and India's GDP data is the most famous case. Years ago he and Ila Patnaik tested the CPI independently. They used the CMIE household survey to derive consumption weights and compared them with the government's CPI weights. They then compared private-sector price data with the government's prices. Both broadly matched, so the CPI can be used with reasonable confidence.
stories.insight: Before building anything on a statistic, verify its foundations yourself. Distrust is the sensible default for government data, but the exceptions can be found empirically, and you should not simply assume them.
stories.quote: the same government that fares poorly on the police and the judiciary and the air quality in North India will also fare poorly in statistical measurement and the release of data.

stories.topic: RBI's Early Decades and a Reform Found, Then Lost
stories.summary: Ajay says that in the bad old days the RBI was not a real central bank. It was a central planning agency and a handmaiden of the government, grabbing money from the formal financial system and repressing it. In the early 1990s C. Rangarajan and deputy governor Tarapore rethought the RBI from scratch. By the time Ajay met them, they knew India needed an open capital account, a floating exchange rate and an inflation target. Then the RBI slid into a long socialist period of detailed micro-control, exchange-rate control, closed accounts and no accountability for inflation. During that period the intellectual leadership moved to academia and the Ministry of Finance.
stories.insight: Institutional progress is not linear. Good ideas can be understood inside an institution and then abandoned, and reform sometimes has to be carried by people outside it until the moment is right.
stories.quote: Like really, when you look at it, it was just an awful central planning organization with little by way of redeeming features.

stories.summary: In 2002 Ajay was already talking with Yashwant Sinha about inflation targeting. Sinha's view was that these ideas were far ahead of what India's intelligentsia was discussing. They would need to become normal in Indian intellectual debate before some future finance minister could act on them. Ajay accepted the point. The reform finally became law in 2016.
stories.insight: A reform usually has to win the argument in public debate long before it can win in government. Years of persuasion are part of how policy change actually happens.
stories.quote: they need to become much more normalized in the Indian intellectual debate before some future finance minister can do that. And you know, point well taken. This is the way it should be done.

stories.topic: How the 2007 Boom Discredited the Old RBI
stories.summary: In the mid-2000s boom, foreign capital poured into India, as it does in good times. The rupee should have appreciated, but the RBI tried to fix the exchange rate by buying up dollars. It paid for those dollars in rupees, flooding the domestic economy with money. The result was expansionary monetary policy at exactly the wrong moment, followed by a big inflation crisis. Ajay says this convinced most economists that the old RBI could no longer be accepted.
stories.insight: Trying to control the exchange rate means giving up control of inflation. A central bank chasing several targets ends up failing at the one that matters most.
stories.quote: And so the local economy got flooded with rupees. And so it was expansionary monetary policy at the worst possible time. And that generated a nice big inflation crisis.

stories.topic: FSLRC and the Draft Indian Financial Code
stories.summary: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission was set up in 2011 under Justice Srikrishna. Ajay was hired to lead its research team: 35 people at NIPFP, led jointly with Ila Patnaik. The mandate was to start from zero and replace some sixty messy old laws with one clean law built on consistent definitions. The result, the draft Indian Financial Code, was released in 2013 and included chapters on inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee. P. Chidambaram said it was too big to pass at the end of his government's term, especially without a Rajya Sabha majority.
stories.insight: Government commissions rarely have real technical capacity behind them. Pairing a commission with a serious research team made it possible to redesign financial law from first principles instead of patching the existing mess.
stories.quote: So this is a rare government commission which was backed by technical capability.

stories.topic: Borrowing the Ways and Means Trick
stories.summary: With the law stuck, Ajay and KP Krishnan exchanged emails at about four an hour while Ajay was travelling abroad. They recalled a precedent from the 1990s. Parliament then could not pass a law to stop the RBI from automatically printing money to fund government deficits. So the Ministry of Finance and the RBI signed a public contract instead, the Ways and Means Agreement, with Montek Ahluwalia and C. Rangarajan signing at a public ceremony. Amit adds that it probably helped to have those two particular people in office. Ajay and Krishnan proposed the same approach for inflation targeting: a Monetary Policy Framework Agreement in which the RBI commits to an inflation target and the government commits not to push it in other directions.
stories.insight: When the legislative route is blocked, a public, signed commitment between the two parties can deliver the reform first, and the law can follow later. It works best when enlightened people happen to hold the key posts.
stories.quote: the Ministry of Finance promised to never ask and RBI promised to never give automatic monetization of deficits.

stories.topic: Chidambaram: 'I Leave This to My Successor'
stories.summary: By late 2013 or early 2014, the draft Monetary Policy Framework Agreement had been worked over by KP Krishnan and P. Chidambaram and discussed with Montek Ahluwalia and Manmohan Singh. Chidambaram wrote on the file that it was one of the most important milestones in India's history. He said it should not be done lightly by a lame-duck government and left the decision to the next finance minister, correctly predicting that this would not be him.
stories.insight: Statesmanship can mean declining to take credit for a reform you believe in, so that it carries proper legitimacy when it happens.
stories.quote: Chidambaram had this wonderful grace of writing on file that this is one of the most important milestones in the history of India. And I don't want to do it lightly, and it should not be the work of a lame duck government.

stories.summary: Amit retells a story from his episode with KP Krishnan. Krishnan handed the file to the new Finance Minister, Arun Jaitley, and the next morning Jaitley said, 'Let's do it.' Krishnan was alarmed: this was far-reaching, so had Jaitley actually read it? Slightly irritated, Jaitley replied that if the country's finest economic mind and finest legal mind had said it must be done, who was he to argue? He meant Manmohan Singh and P. Chidambaram. Amit calls this grace across party lines and says it never happened again.
stories.insight: Trust across party lines is a form of institutional capital, and it can disappear quietly. Years of reform work cleared its final hurdle because one politician deferred to his opponents' expertise.
stories.quote: If this country's finest economic mind and finest legal mind have said that this must be done, then who am I to argue?

stories.topic: Erasing 'Temporary Measure' from the RBI Act
stories.summary: Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan signed the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement on 20 February 2015. Ajay regrets it was not done as a public ceremony. In 2016 the RBI Act was amended to include inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee. The 1934 Act's preamble had said that, given the disorganised international monetary system, India's monetary arrangements could not yet be decided, so the RBI was being created 'as a temporary measure.' The 2016 amendment removed those words and replaced them with 'in order to deliver price stability.'
stories.insight: A preamble states an institution's purpose. For more than eighty years the RBI had none; it was a placeholder. Inflation targeting finally gave it one.
stories.quote: it's like there was a child who was a full grown man standing in 2015, but on his forehead was the word, you're a temporary measure, because we haven't yet figured out what to do.

recommendations.item: Never normalize anything or take the world for granted
recommendations.context: Amit's first, non-media recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: Inflation targeting is a rare, elegant piece of good legislation, and gains like that are always under threat. Keep questioning and protect the little good that has been achieved.

recommendations.creator: Joni Mitchell
recommendations.context: Amit's music recommendation to close the episode.
recommendations.reason: Mitchell is a great singer-songwriter and a masterful guitarist and pianist who was ahead of her time. Folk, rock and jazz musicians drew on her work, and she collaborated with Mingus and Pastorius. Blue is his favourite of her albums. Listen on headphones, on a quiet day, alone.

recommendations.creator: John Maynard Keynes
recommendations.context: Amit cites the pamphlet while telling the story of Germany's post-WWI hyperinflation; it is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Keynes argued that the reparations demands were so extreme partly because nobody knew national wealth. That insight helped create the demand for something like GDP.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Amit promises to link it when he touches on how GDP came into being.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great episode on GDP. It tells the full story he only gestures at here.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Ajay credits 'Milton Friedman's 1968 paper' as the source of the episode's central argument about inflation; it is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the origin of the insight that inflation adds noise to price signals, so firms can't tell real changes from monetary ones and make wrong adjustments.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Ajay echoes the essay's title while agreeing with Amit's summary of how markets work; it is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the foundation for seeing prices as the carriers of society's decentralised knowledge, which is why putting noise into prices is so damaging.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay tells listeners to watch it when he explains why central banks need accountability.
recommendations.reason: Inflation targeting is a direct application of public choice theory. Being appointed to run a central bank does not make anyone a good guy, so power has to be checked.

recommendations.reason: It sets out in detail why growth is the only way out of poverty, which is the deeper reason low and stable inflation matters.

recommendations.reason: It is about how policy ideas move through the pipeline over many years, and the inflation-targeting saga illustrates exactly that.

core_ideas.explanation: A single price rising, such as apples after a maggot infestation, is just supply and demand at work. Inflation means nearly everything rising at once. That happens when the amount of money changes relative to the goods and services available: print 20% more money, keep goods the same, and prices go up. The state has a monopoly on money. Today the central bank controls its supply through interest rates, so inflation is directly in the central bank's control.
core_ideas.quote: Now Milton Friedman once famously said inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Is a Tax on the Poor
core_ideas.explanation: Governments can print money to fund popular spending, which works politically, but everyone pays through higher prices. New money is not handed out in proportion to what people already hold, so the poor suffer most. High inflation is something to hold the government accountable for.
core_ideas.quote: the new money that comes into the system is not distributed in proportion to what people already have. So inevitably the poor are the greatest sufferers, which is why I keep reminding people, inflation is a tax on the poor.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Is the Rising Cost of a Basket
core_ideas.explanation: Your personal inflation rate is the cost of what you buy (quantities times prices) tracked month after month. Some items rise and some fall, but that noise averages out. The CPI does this for the whole country. Large household surveys produce average consumption weights, which stay fixed for a couple of years, and each month's prices are plugged in. Nobody's own inflation matches it exactly, but it reflects what is happening to the average household.
core_ideas.quote: But the average overall systematic increase in the cost of your basket is your inflation

core_ideas.concept: The WPI: Not Wholesale, Not Meaningful, Still Useful
core_ideas.explanation: There is nothing wholesale about the Wholesale Price Index. As an index it is meaningless because its weights reflect nobody's consumption basket. Hence nickel sits in it, though nobody eats nickel. Its one good use is as a long-term database of individual component prices. Measure inflation with the CPI.
core_ideas.quote: Use the CPI. CPI is a decent good index and it is meaningful. Use the WPI underlying component prices as a database.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Corrupts the Signals Firms Rely On
core_ideas.explanation: The world keeps changing, and the market's decentralised information processing is how firms read those changes through prices and adapt. Inflation changes prices for reasons unrelated to the real economy. A firm cannot tell whether apples are dearer because they are scarce, because people want more of them, or just because of inflation. High inflation is also variable inflation, with more noise in prices across the economy. Firms get misled into wrong adjustments. Inflation is not the price of growth; low and stable inflation is what makes good growth possible.
core_ideas.quote: So the deep insight is that high inflation messes with the information processing problem of firms.

core_ideas.concept: Finite Adjustment Muscle and the Acid on Contracts
core_ideas.explanation: Adapting is exhausting, and every firm has a limited budget of effort for it. Firms bind themselves to one another through carefully negotiated contracts written in rupees. When inflation changes what a rupee is worth, those contracts have to be renegotiated even though nothing real has changed. That uses up effort that should have gone into responding to real shifts in tastes and technology. It is a depreciation of contracts.
core_ideas.quote: high and variable inflation is the acid that drips on these contracts and destroys their meaning.

core_ideas.explanation: Long-term projects, like a highway tolled for 20 years, depend on assumptions about future interest rates and contracts. High and variable inflation destroys those assumptions, so people stop planning beyond a couple of years. Growth comes from complex multi-year projects, so the country loses out.
core_ideas.quote: In an environment with high and variable inflation, the future gets reduced into the present. Your planning horizon shrinks.

core_ideas.explanation: The whole case for inflation control serves one end: higher GDP growth, because only growth gets a nation out of poverty. The central bank is one player in that larger effort, and its only part is delivering low and stable inflation.
core_ideas.quote: Growth is the greatest god, because our moral imperative as a nation is to tackle poverty. Only growth gets you out of poverty.

core_ideas.concept: A Central Bank Should Have One Job
core_ideas.explanation: The best thing a central bank can do for society is deliver low and stable inflation. Chasing other goals, or having broad discretion that exposes it to other pressures, always comes at the cost of that core job. Keynes's line about economists being humble like dentists is often applied to central bankers: narrow, technical and accountable.
core_ideas.quote: The core dharma of a central bank is to deliver low and stable inflation.

core_ideas.concept: Power Must Be Matched by Accountability: New Zealand, 1987
core_ideas.explanation: Parliament gives the central bank power to create fiat money. A basic rule of public administration is that every grant of power comes with checks. Central banks have a long history of failure, and New Zealand's fix in 1987 was an inflation target written into law. It even paid senior central bank staff a bonus for hitting it. This is a simple principal-agent arrangement with parliament as the principal. Today all advanced economies target inflation, and central banks that miss suffer reputational damage.
core_ideas.quote: it is a fundamental principle of public administration that power should always be matched by accountability mechanisms. There should never be unchecked power.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Targeting Avoids Two Failure Modes
core_ideas.explanation: A central bank controlled by the government produces an election business cycle: rates are held low before polls to create a feel-good mood, and the inflation arrives later. A fully independent central bank invites economists' self-image as good guys who are beyond public choice theory. An inflation target sits between the two. The legislature defines the job and leaves the bank free to do it, but holds it accountable for the result.
core_ideas.quote: Everybody else we do public choice theory. But for us, we're good guys and we should be given a free hand and we should do whatever we want.

core_ideas.explanation: Good central banks set only the short-term interest rate and leave long-term rates, the exchange rate and equity prices to the market. We are all Wicksellian now. Rate changes take a long time to work, like a car that turns long after you move the wheel, so central banks must forecast inflation rather than react to it. In a boom they raise rates and loans get dearer. In a crisis they cut, as the RBI rightly did when the COVID lockdown hit.
core_ideas.quote: So in the engine room, there's only one joystick where you're controlling the short term rate. It's one scalar, so not even a joystick.

core_ideas.explanation: Zero inflation risks deflationary spirals. A 2% target leaves very little room to cut rates in a slump, because rates can't usefully go below zero. India's broken financial system weakens the effect of rate changes, so larger moves are needed, which requires more headroom. Weak transmission also makes hitting an exact number unrealistic, hence the 2-6% band. Two consecutive quarters outside the band require a public letter from the RBI explaining what went wrong and what it will do. The plan was to narrow the band as the financial system improved.
core_ideas.quote: It is an unreasonable task to ask the central bank that get me precisely 4.00. It's not going to happen. So it's better to put a band around that.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay builds Amit's personal inflation basket: 'Vast amounts of bacon, tiny amounts of bread… Amit Bhai is a good devout non vegetarian and he eats bacon as a matter of principle.' When the CMIE survey comes up, Amit asks, 'But no bacon?' Ajay: 'They have some generic categories called meat and fish and so on, but not the subtlety of bacon.'

Ajay suggests a self-employed doctor can simply charge more when prices rise. Amit: 'Except some of your patients die because food is so expensive they can't afford it anymore, and then you have less patients. I'm kidding.' Ajay, already reaching for the research on inflation shocks and infant mortality: 'Don't even get me started.'
Ajay on the WPI's nickel prices ('what human being eats nickel'), and Amit's summary: 'So the wholesale price index is basically not wholesale, not an index, and not a price by itself.'

Ajay's hypothetical contract pays ten lakh rupees per episode 'to the great podcaster.' Amit tells viewers, 'we're not getting any money for this. It's a labor of love.' Ajay then plays Amit renegotiating after 9% inflation: 'see Mr BeerBiceps, he gets paid so much better than me.'

Amit points out the music lyrics slipped into the conversation, such as Ajay's 'Every year is getting shorter, never seem to find the time' and 'running to standstill,' and asks viewers to list every one in the comments: 'If you don't do that, I will be unsatisfied.'
Amit's one-line summary of the case for central bank discipline: 'buggers, we gave you the monopoly on money, you had one job, keep it stable, don't mess with it too much.'
Ajay ties the price system to 'either Hindu or Buddhist philosophy of a world that is ever changing.' The economy's job is to keep understanding that change and reallocating resources accordingly.

Keynes on humility: Ajay first quotes it as central bankers being 'humble like dentists,' then corrects it to economists, noting it always gets applied to central bankers. He extends it: 'we'll treat you like a dentist. If you did a root canal surgery and the tooth works out fine, then we'll give you a bonus.' On advanced economies that skip New Zealand's bonuses: 'Some of them are too polite or too cheap to offer a bonus.'

Montagu Norman, the former Bank of England governor, quoted by Ajay as the model of an unaccountable central banker: 'I don't have reasons, I have my instincts.' Ajay then slips: 'There should be a mystique of central planning… Oh sorry, there should be a mystique of central banking.'
'In all modern central banks, we are all Wicksellian now': Ajay's shorthand for central banks steering by the short-term interest rate rather than by money supply directly.
Amit on who chose India's 2-6% band: 'A little birdie tells me that one of the co hosts of the show is actually the person who decided it… That person isn't me, so who could it be? Wink wink.'

After Ajay says a central bank must be 'penitent' when it misses its target, Amit: 'I love the way you use phrases central banker and penitent in the same sentence. You know, it reminds me of the famous song Please Forgive Me, No Matter What I Do.'

Ajay, half mock-epic and half rueful: 'O ye young readers of Everything is Everything, if you haven't lived in the glory years of 2007 and 1997, you have no idea what economic success looks like. You have just lived in some grim dark days and you have normalized the sadness.'
Amit on their development episode, recorded in the mountains: 'we had to go to the highest place to talk about the highest god.'
Ajay signing off the theory: 'Out of talking about all this, my CPU power has dwindled away. Now I'm a Z80.'
